entries.zh: 右行，圓蓋一，金交椅一， 金水罐一，團黃扇三，紅扇三。
entries.en: On the right, one round canopy, one gold folding chair, one gold water jar, three round yellow fans, and three red fans.
entries.literal: On the right, one round canopy, one gold folding chair, one gold water jar, three round yellow fans, three red fans.

entries.zh: 皆校尉擎執。
entries.en: Guard commandants bore them all.
entries.literal: All were borne by guard commandants.

entries.zh: 殿上左右內使監陳設：左，拂子二， 金唾壺一，金香合一；
entries.en: Within the hall the palace attendants arranged: on the left, two whisk fans, one gold spittoon, and one gold incense box.
entries.literal: Inside the hall, left and right, the Directorate of Palace Attendants set out: on the left, two whisk fans, one gold spittoon, one gold incense box.

entries.zh: 右，拂子二，金唾盂一，金香爐一。
entries.en: On the right, two whisk fans, one gold spittoon bowl, and one gold incense burner.
entries.literal: On the right, two whisk fans, one gold spittoon bowl, one gold incense burner.

entries.zh: 皆內使擎執。
entries.en: Palace attendants bore them all.
entries.literal: All were borne by palace attendants.

entries.zh: 和聲郎 陳樂於丹墀文武官拜位之南，其器數詳見《樂志》內。
entries.en: Harmony Officers stationed musicians south of the civil and military officials' obeisance marks on the red courtyard; instrument counts appear in the Treatise on Music.
entries.literal: Harmony Officers set out music south of the civil and military officials' obeisance positions on the red courtyard; the number of instruments is detailed in the Treatise on Music.

entries.zh: 皇帝儀仗：吳元年十二月辛酉，中書左相國李善長率禮官以即位禮儀進。
entries.en: The emperor's ceremonial train: On the xinyou day of the twelfth month of the first Wu year, Left Chancellor Li Shanchang led the ritual officials in presenting the enthronement rites.
entries.literal: The emperor's ceremonial regalia: On the xinyou day of the twelfth month of the first year of Wu, Left Chancellor of the Secretariat Li Shanchang led the ritual officials in presenting the enthronement ceremonies.

entries.zh: 是 日清晨，拱衛司陳設鹵簿，列甲士於午門外之東西，列旗仗於奉天門外之東西。
entries.en: At dawn that day the Imperial Escort Directorate arrayed the guard of honor, posting armored soldiers to the east and west of the Meridian Gate and ceremonial banners to the east and west of the Gate of Supreme Harmony.
entries.literal: That morning at dawn the Imperial Escort Directorate set out the guard of honor, lining armored soldiers east and west outside the Meridian Gate and arraying banners and regalia east and west outside the Gate of Supreme Harmony.

entries.zh: 龍旗十二，分左右，用甲士十二人。
entries.en: Twelve dragon banners, six to each side, borne by twelve armored soldiers.
entries.literal: Twelve dragon banners, divided left and right, with twelve armored soldiers.

entries.zh: 北斗旗一、纛一居前，豹尾一居後，俱用甲 士三人。
entries.en: One Big Dipper banner and one command banner led the way; one leopard-tail standard brought up the rear—three armored soldiers for each.
entries.literal: One Big Dipper banner and one great banner went before, one leopard-tail standard behind, each with three armored soldiers.

entries.zh: 虎豹各二，馴象六，分左右。
entries.en: Two tiger and two leopard figures apiece, with six trained elephants, arrayed to left and right.
entries.literal: Two each of tiger and leopard figures, six trained elephants, divided left and right.

entries.zh: 布旗六十四：門旗、日旗、月旗，青龍、 白虎、風、雲、雷、雨、江、河、淮、濟旗，天馬、天祿、白澤、朱雀、玄武等 旗，木、火、土、金、水五星旗，五嶽旗，熊旗，鸞旗及二十八宿旗，各六行；
entries.en: Sixty-four cloth banners in all—gate, sun, and moon; Azure Dragon and White Tiger; wind, cloud, thunder, and rain; the Yangtze, Yellow River, Huai, and Ji; Heavenly Horse, Heavenly Blessing, White Marsh, Vermilion Bird, and Dark Warrior; the banners of the five elements and five sacred peaks; bear and phoenix; and the twenty-eight lunar mansions—each arrayed in six rows.
entries.literal: Sixty-four cloth banners: gate, sun, and moon banners; Azure Dragon, White Tiger, wind, cloud, thunder, rain, Yangtze, Yellow River, Huai, and Ji banners; Heavenly Horse, Heavenly Blessing, White Marsh, Vermilion Bird, Dark Warrior, and other banners; Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water Five Stars banners; Five Sacred Peaks banners; bear and phoenix banners; and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions banners, six rows each.

entries.zh: 每旗用甲士五人，一人執旗，四人執弓弩。
entries.en: Each banner was manned by five armored soldiers—one to carry it, four with bows and crossbows.
entries.literal: Each banner employed five armored soldiers: one bore the banner, four bore bows and crossbows.

entries.zh: 設五輅於奉天門外：玉輅居中，左金 輅，次革輅，右象輅，次木輅，俱並列。
entries.en: Five imperial carriages stood outside the Gate of Supreme Harmony: the jade carriage at center; to its left the gold carriage and then the leather carriage; to its right the ivory carriage and then the wood carriage—all aligned abreast.
entries.literal: Five imperial carriages were set outside the Gate of Supreme Harmony: the jade carriage in the center; to the left the gold carriage, then the leather carriage; to the right the ivory carriage, then the wood carriage—all ranged in parallel.

entries.zh: 丹墀左右布黃麾仗、黃蓋、華蓋、曲蓋、 紫方傘、紅方傘、雉扇、朱團扇、羽葆幢、豹尾、龍頭竿、信幡、傳教幡、告止 幡、絳引幡、戟氅、戈氅、儀鍠氅等，各三行。
entries.en: On either side of the red courtyard stood yellow command regalia, yellow and flowered canopies, curved canopies, purple and red square umbrellas, pheasant-tail and vermilion round fans, feathered canopy staffs, leopard-tail and dragon-head poles, trust, instruction, stop, and crimson guide banners, and halberd, dagger-axe, and ceremonial bell pennants—three rows apiece.
entries.literal: To left and right of the red courtyard were arrayed yellow command regalia, yellow canopies, flowered canopies, curved canopies, purple square umbrellas, red square umbrellas, pheasant-tail fans, vermilion round fans, feathered canopy staffs, leopard-tail standards, dragon-head poles, trust banners, instruction banners, stop banners, crimson guide banners, halberd pennants, dagger-axe pennants, ceremonial bell pennants, and the like, three rows each.

entries.zh: 丹陛左右陳幢節、響節、金節、 燭籠、青龍白虎幢、班劍、吾杖、立瓜、臥瓜、儀刀、鐙杖、戟、骨朵、朱雀玄 武幢等，各三行。
entries.en: Flanking the red steps were canopy staffs, sounding and gold staffs, candle lanterns, Azure Dragon and White Tiger canopy staffs, court swords, ceremonial staffs, standing and reclining melons, ceremonial blades, stirrup staffs, halberds, maces, and Vermilion Bird and Dark Warrior canopy staffs—again three rows each.
entries.literal: To left and right of the red steps were displayed canopy staffs, sounding staffs, gold staffs, candle lanterns, Azure Dragon and White Tiger canopy staffs, court swords, ceremonial staffs, standing melons, reclining melons, ceremonial blades, stirrup staffs, halberds, maces, Vermilion Bird and Dark Warrior canopy staffs, and the like, three rows each.

entries.zh: 殿門左右設圓蓋一、金交椅、金腳踏、水盆、水罐、團黃扇、 紅扇。
entries.en: Beside the hall doors stood a round canopy on each side, a gold folding chair, gold footrests, basins and jars for water, round yellow fans, and red fans.
entries.literal: To left and right of the hall doors were set one round canopy each, a gold folding chair, gold footrests, water basins, water jars, round yellow fans, and red fans.

entries.zh: 皆校尉擎執。
entries.en: Guard commandants bore them all.
entries.literal: All were borne by guard commandants.

entries.zh: 三年，命制郊丘祭祀拜褥。
entries.en: In the third year the court ordered kneeling mats made for suburban altar rites.
entries.literal: In the third year an order was issued to make kneeling mats for suburban altar sacrifices.

entries.zh: 郊丘用席表蒲裏爲褥，宗廟、社稷、先農、山川 用紅文綺表紅木棉布裏爲褥。
entries.en: Suburban altars used mats faced with rush matting and padded with rush; the ancestral temple, altars of soil and grain, the god of agriculture, and mountain-and-river sacrifices used mats faced with red patterned silk and lined with red cotton cloth.
entries.literal: For suburban altars, mats with rush matting on the outside and rush padding within were used; for the ancestral temple, altars of soil and grain, the god of agriculture, and mountains and rivers, mats with red patterned silk on the outside and red wood-cotton cloth within were used.

entries.zh: 十二年，命禮部增設丹墀儀仗，黃傘、華蓋、曲蓋、 紫方傘、紅方傘各二，雉扇、紅團扇各四，羽葆幢、龍頭竿、絳引、傳教、告止、 信幡各六，戟氅、戈氅、儀鍠氅各十。
entries.en: In the twelfth year the Ministry of Rites was told to expand red-courtyard regalia: two each of yellow, flowered, and curved canopies and purple and red square umbrellas; four pheasant-tail and red round fans apiece; six each of feathered canopy staffs, dragon-head poles, and crimson guide, instruction, stop, and trust banners; and ten each of halberd, dagger-axe, and ceremonial bell pennants.
entries.literal: In the twelfth year the Ministry of Rites was ordered to add ceremonial regalia on the red courtyard: two each of yellow umbrellas, flowered canopies, curved canopies, purple square umbrellas, and red square umbrellas; four each of pheasant-tail fans and red round fans; six each of feathered canopy staffs, dragon-head poles, crimson guide, instruction, stop, and trust banners; ten each of halberd, dagger-axe, and ceremonial bell pennants.

entries.zh: 親王儀仗，洪武六年定：宮門外設方色旗二，青色白澤旗二，執人服隨旗色， 並戎服。
entries.en: Imperial princes' ceremonial train, fixed in Hongwu's sixth year: outside the palace gate stood two directional-color banners and two green White Marsh banners, bearers in military dress colored to match.
entries.literal: Imperial princes' ceremonial regalia, fixed in the sixth year of Hongwu: outside the palace gate two directional-color banners and two green White Marsh banners were set; bearers dressed according to banner color, all in military dress.

entries.zh: 殿下，絳引幡二，戟氅二，戈氅二，儀鍠氅二，皆校尉執。
entries.en: Below the hall: two crimson guide banners and two each of halberd, dagger-axe, and ceremonial bell pennants, all borne by guard commandants.
entries.literal: Below the hall: two crimson guide banners, two halberd pennants, two dagger-axe pennants, two ceremonial bell pennants—all borne by guard commandants.

entries.zh: 殿前，班劍 二，吾杖二，立瓜二，臥瓜二，儀刀二，鐙杖二，骨朵二，斧二，響節八，皆校 尉執。
entries.en: Before the hall: two each of court swords, ceremonial staffs, standing and reclining melons, ceremonial blades, stirrup staffs, maces, and axes, plus eight sounding staffs—all borne by guard commandants.
entries.literal: Before the hall: two court swords, two ceremonial staffs, two standing melons, two reclining melons, two ceremonial blades, two stirrup staffs, two maces, two axes, eight sounding staffs—all borne by guard commandants.

entries.zh: 殿門，交椅一，腳踏一，水罐一，水盆一，團扇四，蓋二，皆校尉執。
entries.en: At the hall doors: one folding chair, footrest, water jar and basin, four round fans, and two canopies—all borne by guard commandants.
entries.literal: At the hall doors: one folding chair, one footrest, one water jar, one water basin, four round fans, two canopies—all borne by guard commandants.

entries.zh: 殿 上，拂子二，香爐一，香合一，唾壺一，唾盂一。
entries.en: Within the hall: two whisk fans, one incense burner and box, and one spittoon pot and bowl.
entries.literal: Inside the hall: two whisk fans, one incense burner, one incense box, one spittoon pot, one spittoon bowl.

entries.zh: 十六年詔，親王儀仗內交椅、 盆、罐用銀者，悉改用金。
entries.en: In the sixteenth year an edict required that silver folding chairs, basins, and jars in princes' ceremonial trains be replaced with gold.
entries.literal: In the sixteenth year an edict ordered that folding chairs, basins, and jars of silver in imperial princes' ceremonial regalia all be changed to gold.

entries.zh: 建文四年，禮部言，親王儀仗合增紅油絹銷金雨傘一， 紅紗燈籠、紅油紙燈籠各四，敔燈二，大小銅角四。
entries.en: In Jianwen's fourth year the Ministry of Rites proposed adding to princes' trains one red-oil-silk gold-brocaded rain umbrella, four red gauze and four red-oil-paper lanterns, two yi-lamps, and four bronze horns large and small.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Jianwen the Ministry of Rites said imperial princes' ceremonial regalia should add one red-oil-silk gold-brocaded rain umbrella, four each of red gauze lanterns and red-oil-paper lanterns, two yi-lamps, and four large and small bronze horns.

entries.zh: 從之。
entries.en: The court approved.
entries.literal: The proposal was approved.

entries.zh: 永樂三年命工部，親 王儀仗內紅銷金傘，仍用寶珠龍文。
entries.en: In Yongle's third year the Works Ministry was told that princes' red gold-brocaded umbrellas should retain pearl-and-dragon ornament.
entries.literal: In the third year of Yongle the Ministry of Works was ordered that red gold-brocaded umbrellas in imperial princes' ceremonial regalia should still use pearl-and-dragon designs.

entries.zh: 凡世子儀仗同。
entries.en: The ceremonial train of a prince's heir followed the same rules.
entries.literal: The ceremonial regalia of a prince's heir was the same in all respects.

entries.zh: 卷六十四 志第四十
entries.en: Volume 64, Treatise 40
entries.literal: Volume 64, Treatise 40

entries.zh: 有虞氏御天下，車服以庸。
entries.en: When the House of Yu held the realm, carriage and apparel were assigned according to merit and rank.
entries.literal: When the House of Yu ruled All-under-Heaven, carriages and dress were regulated by merit.

entries.zh: 夏則黻冕致美。
entries.en: Under the Xia, embroidered caps and ceremonial dress were carried to their finest point.
entries.literal: In Xia, patterned caps and robes reached their utmost refinement.

entries.zh: 商則大輅示儉。
entries.en: Under the Shang, the Great Carriage was made to exemplify restraint.
entries.literal: In Shang, the Great Carriage displayed frugality.

entries.zh: 成周有巾車、典 輅、弁師、司服之職，天子以之表式萬邦，而服車五乘，下逮臣民。
entries.en: In mature Zhou there were officers for carriage caps, state carriages, caps, and court dress; the Son of Heaven used them to display the standard for all lands, with five grades of service carriages reaching down to officials and the people.
entries.literal: In the completion of Zhou there were the offices of Cap-Maker of Carriages, Director of Carriages, Cap-Master, and Director of Apparel; the Son of Heaven thereby set the pattern for the myriad states, while five grades of service carriages extended down to ministers and commoners.

entries.zh: 漢承秦制， 御金根爲乘輿，服袀玄以承大祀。
entries.en: The Han took over Qin institutions, riding the Golden Root carriage as the imperial conveyance and wearing dark sacrificial robes for the major state rites.
entries.literal: Han inherited the Qin system, using the Golden Root as the imperial carriage and wearing dark ceremonial dress for the great sacrifices.

entries.zh: 東都乃有九斿、雲罕、旒冕、絇屨之儀物， 踵事增華，日新代異。
entries.en: At the Eastern Capital there appeared regalia such as the nine-tasseled banners, cloud canopy, jeweled crown, and knotted court shoes, with each reign adding further splendor until the forms changed from age to age.
entries.literal: The Eastern Capital then had ritual objects such as the nine tassels, cloud canopy, tasseled crown, and knotted shoes, each generation piling ornament upon ornament, renewing and altering them day by day.

entries.zh: 江左偏安，玉輅棲寶鳳，採旄銜金龍。
entries.en: In the partial regime south of the Yangzi, jade carriages carried jeweled phoenixes, and colored streamers were fitted with golden dragons.
entries.literal: The south of the Yangzi held only a partial realm; the jade carriage bore jeweled phoenixes, and colored pennants held golden dragons in their mouths.

entries.zh: 其服冕也，或飾翡 翠、珊瑚、雜珠。
entries.en: Their ceremonial crowns were sometimes set with jadeite, coral, and mixed pearls.
entries.literal: Their ceremonial crowns were sometimes adorned with jadeite, coral, and assorted pearls.

entries.zh: 豈古所謂法駕、法服者哉？
entries.en: Could these still be what the ancients meant by the prescribed imperial carriage and prescribed court dress?
entries.literal: How could these be what antiquity called the statutory carriage and statutory dress?

entries.zh: 唐武德間著車輿、衣服之制，上得 兼下，下不得擬上。
entries.en: During Tang Wude, statutes for carriages and dress were issued: higher ranks could include lower forms, but lower ranks could not adopt higher ones.
entries.literal: In the Wude era of Tang, regulations for carriages and clothing were promulgated: those above might encompass those below, but those below might not imitate those above.

entries.zh: 宋初，袞冕不綴珠玉。
entries.en: Early in the Song, the dragon robe and crown bore no strings of pearls and jade.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Song, the dragon robe and crown were not strung with pearls and jade.

entries.zh: 政和中詔修車輅，並建旂常，議禮局 所釐定，用爲成憲。
entries.en: In the Zhenghe reign an edict called for restoring the state carriages and setting up the banner regalia; the Ritual Deliberation Bureau fixed the forms, and these became permanent law.
entries.literal: In the Zhenghe era an edict ordered the repair of state carriages and the establishment of banner regalia; what the Bureau for Deliberation on Rites determined was taken as settled statute.

entries.zh: 元制，郊祀則駕玉輅，服袞冕；
entries.en: Under Yuan practice, at suburban sacrifice the emperor rode the jade carriage and wore the dragon robe and crown;
entries.literal: Under Yuan institutions, for suburban sacrifice one rode the jade carriage and wore the dragon robe and crown;

entries.zh: 巡幸，或乘象轎，四時質孫 之服，各隨其宜。
entries.en: on imperial tours one sometimes used an elephant palanquin, while the plain and colored seasonal garments were worn as each occasion required.
entries.literal: on tours of inspection one sometimes rode an elephant palanquin, and the plain and colored garments of the four seasons were each worn as appropriate.

entries.zh: 明太祖甫有天下，考定邦禮，車服尚質。
entries.en: As soon as the Ming Founder secured the realm, he reviewed and fixed the state rituals, keeping carriages and dress plain.
entries.literal: When the Ming Founder had just gained All-under-Heaven, he examined and fixed the state rites, and carriages and dress valued simplicity.

entries.zh: 酌古通今，合乎禮意。
entries.en: Drawing on antiquity while suiting the present, they conformed to ritual propriety.
entries.literal: Weighing antiquity and connecting with the present, they accorded with ritual intent.

entries.zh: 迄於世宗，耤田造耕根，燕居服燕弁，講武用武弁，更爲忠靖冠以風有位，爲保 和冠以親宗藩，亦一王之制也。
entries.en: By the Shizong reign, the ploughing-field rite produced the Plough-Root carriage; informal residence called for the casual court cap and military drills for the martial cap; the Zhongjing cap was introduced to guide officials in office and the Baohe cap to draw the imperial clan and feudatories near—institutions proper to one dynasty as well.
entries.literal: Down to the Shizong Emperor, ploughing fields produced the Plough-Root carriage; at ease in the palace one wore the casual cap; for martial instruction one used the military cap; further there were made the Zhongjing cap to admonish those in office and the Baohe cap to draw near imperial clans and feudatories—also the institutions of a single royal house.

entries.zh: 若夫前代傘扇、鞍勒之儀，門戟、旌節之屬，鹹 別等威，至宋加密。
entries.en: As for earlier protocols for parasols, fans, saddles, and bridles, gate halberds, banners, and tally staffs, each rank had its own display of authority, and the Song tightened these distinctions further.
entries.literal: As for the rites of former ages concerning parasols, fans, saddles, and bridles, gate-halberds, banners, and tally-staves, all distinguished grades of majesty, and by the Song these were drawn ever tighter.

entries.zh: 明初儉德開基，宮殿落成，不用文石甃地。
entries.en: Early Ming was founded on frugal virtue: when the palaces were finished, no figured stone was laid for paving.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Ming, frugal virtue founded the dynasty; when palaces were completed, patterned stone was not used to pave the floors.

entries.zh: 以此坊民，武臣 猶有飾金龍於牀幔，馬廄用九五間數，而豪民亦或熔金爲酒器，飾以玉珠。
entries.en: Even with this restraint on the people, military officers still put golden dragons on bed curtains, stables were built with the nine-by-five bay pattern, and wealthy families sometimes cast gold wine vessels set with jade beads.
entries.literal: By this to restrain the people, yet military officers still ornamented bed curtains with golden dragons, stables used the nine-five bay count, and powerful families also sometimes melted gold into wine vessels and adorned them with jade beads.

entries.zh: 太祖 皆重懲其弊。
entries.en: The Founder punished every such abuse severely.
entries.literal: The Founder in every case severely punished these abuses.

entries.zh: 乃命儒臣稽古講禮，定官民服舍器用制度。
entries.en: He then ordered scholar-officials to study antiquity and expound ritual, establishing regulations for the dress, housing, and utensils of officials and commoners.
entries.literal: He then ordered Confucian officials to examine antiquity and expound ritual, fixing the institutions for dress, dwellings, and utensils of officials and commoners.

entries.zh: 歷代守之，遞有禁例。
entries.en: Each reign upheld them, and prohibitions accumulated over time.
entries.literal: Each generation preserved them, and in succession there were prohibitory precedents.

entries.zh: 茲更以朝家冊寶、中外符信及宮室器用之等差，附敘於後焉。
entries.en: What follows also records the gradations of court seals and treasures, domestic and foreign credentials, and palace furnishings and utensils.
entries.literal: Here further, with the gradations of court seals and treasures, internal and external tallies and credentials, and palace furnishings and utensils, these are appended and narrated afterward.

entries.zh: 天子車輅：明初大朝會，則拱衛司設五輅於奉天門，玉居中，左金，次革， 右象，次木。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven's state carriages: in early Ming, at great court assemblies the Imperial Guard Office arrayed the five carriages before the Gate of Receiving Heaven, with the jade carriage in the center, gold to the left, then leather, ivory to the right, then wood.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven's state carriages: at the beginning of Ming, at great court assemblies the Imperial Guard Office set out the five carriages before the Gate of Receiving Heaven—jade in the center, to the left gold, next leather, to the right ivory, next wood.

entries.zh: 駕出則乘玉輅，後有腰輿，以八人載之。
entries.en: When the emperor went forth he rode the jade carriage, with a waist sedan carried by eight bearers behind.
entries.literal: When the imperial procession set out he rode the jade carriage; behind was a waist sedan borne by eight men.

entries.zh: 其後太祖考《周禮》五輅， 以詢儒臣，曰：「玉輅太侈，何若祗用木輅？」
entries.en: Later the Founder studied the five carriages in the 《Rites of Zhou》 and asked the scholar-officials, "The jade carriage is too lavish—why not use only the wooden carriage?"
entries.literal: Afterward the Founder examined the five carriages in the 《Rites of Zhou》 and questioned the Confucian officials, saying, "The jade carriage is too extravagant—how about using only the wooden carriage?"

entries.zh: 博士詹同對曰：「孔子云『乘殷 之輅』，即木輅也。」
entries.en: Academician Zhan Tong answered, "Confucius said 'ride the carriage of Yin'—that means the wooden carriage."
entries.literal: Academician Zhan Tong replied, "Confucius said 'ride the carriage of Yin'—that is the wooden carriage."

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「以玉飾車，古惟祀天用之，常乘宜用殷輅。
entries.en: The Founder said, "Jade ornament on a carriage was used in antiquity only when sacrificing to Heaven; for everyday riding the Yin carriage is appropriate.
entries.literal: The Founder said, "To ornament a carriage with jade—in antiquity this was used only for sacrificing to Heaven; for ordinary riding one should use the Yin carriage.

entries.zh: 然 祀天之際，玉輅未備，木輅亦未爲不可。」
entries.en: Yet if the jade carriage is not ready when sacrificing to Heaven, the wooden carriage is not out of the question."
entries.literal: Yet at the time of sacrificing to Heaven, if the jade carriage is not ready, the wooden carriage is also not impermissible."

entries.zh: 參政張昶曰：「木輅，戎輅也，不可 以祀天。」
entries.en: Participating Secretary Zhang Chang said, "The wooden carriage is the military carriage and cannot be used for sacrifice to Heaven."
entries.literal: Participating Secretary Zhang Chang said, "The wooden carriage is the military carriage and may not be used to sacrifice to Heaven."

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「孔子斟酌四代禮樂，以爲萬世法，木輅寧不可祀？
entries.en: The Founder said, "Confucius weighed the rites and music of four dynasties to set the model for all time—why should the wooden carriage be unfit for sacrifice?
entries.literal: The Founder said, "Confucius weighed the ritual and music of four dynasties to make the law for ten thousand generations—how could the wooden carriage not be used for sacrifice?

entries.zh: 祀在誠 敬，豈泥儀文。」
entries.en: Sacrifice rests on sincerity and reverence, not on clinging to ceremonial detail."
entries.literal: Sacrifice lies in sincerity and reverence—how can one be bound to ceremonial forms?"

entries.zh: 洪武元年，有司奏乘輿服御，應以金飾，詔用銅。
entries.en: In Hongwu 1 the responsible offices proposed gilding the imperial carriage and regalia; the emperor ordered copper instead.
entries.literal: In the first year of Hongwu, the responsible offices memorialized that the imperial carriage and apparel should be ornamented with gold; an edict ordered copper instead.

entries.zh: 有司言費小 不足惜。
entries.en: The offices said the cost was trifling and not worth worrying over.
entries.literal: The offices said the expense was small and not worth sparing.

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「朕富有四海，豈吝乎此？
entries.en: The Founder said, "I possess all within the four seas—would I begrudge this?
entries.literal: The Founder said, "I possess the four seas in wealth—how could I be stingy about this?

entries.zh: 第儉約非身先無以率下，且奢泰之 習，未有不由小而至大者也。」
entries.en: But unless the ruler leads in frugality himself, he cannot guide those below; and the habit of extravagance always grows from small things to great."
entries.literal: Only frugality, if the ruler does not take the lead himself, cannot guide those below; moreover the habit of extravagance has never failed to grow from small beginnings to great ones."

entries.zh: 六年，命禮官考五輅制，爲木輅二乘。
entries.en: In the sixth year he ordered ritual officials to study the five-carriage regulations and commission two wooden carriages.
entries.literal: In the sixth year he ordered ritual officials to examine the institutions of the five carriages and make two wooden carriages.

entries.zh: 一以丹漆， 祭祀用之；
entries.en: One was lacquered cinnabar red for sacrifices;
entries.literal: One was finished in cinnabar lacquer, for use in sacrifice;

entries.zh: 一以皮鞔，行幸用之。
entries.en: one was leather-covered for imperial tours.
entries.literal: one was covered in leather, for use on imperial tours.

entries.zh: 是冬，大輅成。
entries.en: That winter the Great Carriage was finished.
entries.literal: That winter the Great Carriage was completed.

entries.zh: 命更造大輅一，象輅十，中宮 輅一，後宮車十，飾俱以鳳。
entries.en: He ordered one more Great Carriage, ten ivory carriages, one central-palace carriage, and ten rear-palace carriages, all decorated with phoenixes.
entries.literal: He ordered the further manufacture of one Great Carriage, ten ivory carriages, one central-palace carriage, and ten rear-palace carriages, all ornamented with phoenixes.

entries.zh: 以將幸中立府，故造之，非常制也。
entries.en: They were built because he was about to visit the Neutral Capital and were not part of the regular establishment.
entries.literal: Because he was about to visit the Neutral Capital, these were made; they were not the regular institutions.

entries.zh: 二十六年，始 定鹵簿大駕之制。
entries.en: In the twenty-sixth year the regulations for the full imperial guard of honor were first established.
entries.literal: In the twenty-sixth year the institutions of the full guard of honor for the great imperial procession were first fixed.

entries.zh: 玉輅一，大輅一，九龍車一，步輦一。
entries.en: There were one jade carriage, one Great Carriage, one Nine-Dragon Carriage, and one hand sedan.
entries.literal: One jade carriage, one Great Carriage, one Nine-Dragon Carriage, and one hand sedan.

entries.zh: 後罷九龍車。
entries.en: The Nine-Dragon Carriage was later discontinued.
entries.literal: Later the Nine-Dragon Carriage was abolished.

entries.zh: 永樂三年 更定鹵簿大駕，有大輅、玉輅、大馬輦、小馬輦、步輦、大涼步輦、板轎各一， 具服、幄殿各一。
entries.en: In Yongle 3 the great imperial guard of honor was revised to include one each of the Great Carriage, jade carriage, large and small horse sedans, hand sedan, large cool hand sedan, and board palanquin, plus one full-dress pavilion and one canopy hall.
entries.literal: In the third year of Yongle the full guard of honor for the great procession was revised: there were one each of the Great Carriage, jade carriage, large horse sedan, small horse sedan, hand sedan, large cool hand sedan, and board palanquin, and one each of the full-dress pavilion and canopy hall.

entries.zh: 耕根車，世宗朝始造。
entries.en: The Plough-Root Carriage was first built in the Shizong reign.
entries.literal: The Plough-Root Carriage was first made in the Shizong reign.

entries.zh: 漢有耕車，晉曰耕根車，俱天子親耕所用。
entries.en: The Han had a ploughing carriage; the Jin called it the Plough-Root Carriage—both were used when the Son of Heaven ploughed in person.
entries.literal: Han had the ploughing carriage; Jin called it the Plough-Root Carriage—both were what the Son of Heaven used for personal ploughing.

entries.zh: 嘉靖十年， 帝將耕耤田，詔造耕根車。
entries.en: In Jiajing 10, as the emperor was about to plough the sacred field, an edict ordered the Plough-Root Carriage built.
entries.literal: In the tenth year of Jiajing, when the emperor was about to plough the sacred field, an edict ordered the manufacture of the Plough-Root Carriage.

entries.zh: 禮官上言：「考《大明集禮》，耕耤用宋制，乘玉輅， 以耕根車載耒耜同行。
entries.en: Ritual officials reported: "According to the Collected Rites of the Great Ming, the sacred-field ploughing follows Song practice: the emperor rides the jade carriage while the Plough-Root Carriage carries the plough and hoe alongside.
entries.literal: Ritual officials memorialized: "Examining the Collected Rites of the Great Ming, ploughing the sacred field follows Song institutions: ride the jade carriage, and let the Plough-Root Carriage carry the plough and hoe traveling together.

entries.zh: 今考儀注，順天府官奉耒耜及穜稑種置彩輿，先於祭 前二日而出。
entries.en: Under current ritual protocols, Shuntian officials present the plough and hoe and place the early and late grain seeds in a colored carriage sent out two days before the sacrifice.
entries.literal: Now examining the ritual protocols, Shuntian prefectural officials present the plough and hoe and place the early and late grain seeds in a colored carriage, which goes out two days before the sacrifice.

entries.zh: 今用耕根車以載耒耜，宜令造車，於祭祀日早進呈，置耒耜，先玉 輅以行。
entries.en: The Plough-Root Carriage should now carry the plough and hoe: order the carriage built, present it early on the sacrifice day with the tools aboard, and send it out ahead of the jade carriage.
entries.literal: Now to use the Plough-Root Carriage to carry the plough and hoe, it is fitting to order the carriage made, presented early on the sacrifice day, place the plough and hoe, and go forth before the jade carriage.

entries.zh: 第稽諸禮書，只有圖式，而無高廣尺寸。
entries.en: But the ritual books give only diagrams, with no height or width measurements.
entries.literal: Only, examining the ritual books, there are diagram forms but no height and width dimensions.

entries.zh: 宜依今置車式差小，通用青質。」
entries.en: It should follow the present service-carriage form, made somewhat smaller and finished entirely in blue."
entries.literal: It is fitting to follow the present service-carriage form made somewhat smaller, universally using blue material."

entries.zh: 從之。
entries.en: The proposal was approved.
entries.literal: This was followed.

entries.zh: 轎者，肩行之車。
entries.en: A palanquin is a shoulder-borne carriage.
entries.literal: The palanquin is a vehicle carried on the shoulders.

entries.zh: 宋中興以後，皇后嘗乘龍肩輿。
entries.en: After the Song restoration, empresses sometimes rode a dragon shoulder palanquin.
entries.literal: After the restoration of Song, the empress sometimes rode a dragon shoulder carriage.

entries.zh: 又以征伐，道路險阻，詔 百官乘轎，名曰：「竹轎子」，亦曰：「竹輿」。
entries.en: During campaigns over difficult terrain, an edict also required officials to ride palanquins called "bamboo palanquins" or "bamboo carriages."
entries.literal: Also because of campaigns, when roads were perilous, an edict ordered all officials to ride palanquins, named the "bamboo palanquin," also called the "bamboo carriage."

entries.zh: 元皇帝用象轎，駕以二象。
entries.en: Yuan emperors used elephant palanquins drawn by two elephants.
entries.literal: Yuan emperors used elephant palanquins, driven by two elephants.

entries.zh: 至用紅 板轎，則自明始也。
entries.en: The red board palanquin, however, dates only from the Ming.
entries.literal: As for using the red board palanquin, this began only with Ming.

entries.zh: 其制，高六尺九寸有奇。
entries.en: It stood a little over six feet nine inches high.
entries.literal: Its form was a little over six feet nine inches high.

entries.zh: 頂紅髹。
entries.en: The top was red-lacquered.
entries.literal: The top was lacquered red.

entries.zh: 近頂裝圓匡蜊房窗，鍍金 銅火焰寶，帶仰覆蓮座，四角鍍金銅雲朵。
entries.en: Near the top was a round frame with honeycomb windows, gilt-bronze flame jewels with lotus seats, and gilt-bronze clouds at the four corners.
entries.literal: Near the top was fitted a round frame with honeycomb windows, gilt-bronze flame jewels, with upturned and downturned lotus seats, and gilt-bronze clouds at the four corners.

entries.zh: 轎槓二，前後以鍍金銅龍頭、龍尾裝 釘，有黃絨墜角索。
entries.en: It had two carrying poles fitted front and rear with gilt-bronze dragon heads and tails, with yellow plush corner ropes.
entries.literal: Two palanquin poles, front and rear fitted with gilt-bronze dragon heads and tails, with yellow plush corner-drop ropes.

entries.zh: 四周紅髹板，左右門二，用鍍金銅釘鉸。
entries.en: The sides were red-lacquered panels with two doors left and right on gilt-bronze hinges.
entries.literal: On all four sides were red-lacquered boards; to left and right were two doors, using gilt-bronze nail hinges.

entries.zh: 轎內紅髹匡坐椅一， 福壽板一併褥。
entries.en: Inside was one red-lacquered chair with a fortune-and-longevity panel and cushions.
entries.literal: Within the palanquin was one red-lacquered frame chair, one fortune-longevity panel together with cushions.

entries.zh: 椅內黃織金綺靠坐褥，四周椅裙，下鋪席並踏褥。
entries.en: The chair held yellow gold-woven damask back and seat cushions with a skirt on all four sides, with mat and step cushion below.
entries.literal: Within the chair were yellow gold-woven damask back and seat cushions, a chair skirt on all four sides; below were spread mat and step cushion.

entries.zh: 有黃絹轎衣、 油絹雨衣各一，青氈衣，紅氈緣條雲子。
entries.en: There were one yellow silk cover and one oiled-silk rain cover, a blue felt cover, and red felt borders with cloud motifs.
entries.literal: There were one each of yellow silk palanquin cover and oiled-silk rain cover, a blue felt cover, and red felt border strips with cloud motifs.

entries.zh: 嘉靖十三年謁廟，帝及后妃俱乘肩輿出 宮，至奉天門降輿升輅。
entries.en: In Jiajing 13, when visiting the temple, the emperor and consorts left the palace in shoulder palanquins, then at the Gate of Receiving Heaven dismounted and boarded the state carriage.
entries.literal: In the thirteenth year of Jiajing, when visiting the temple, the emperor and consorts all rode shoulder carriages out of the palace; at the Gate of Receiving Heaven they descended from the carriage and mounted the state carriage.

entries.zh: 隆慶四年設郊祀慶成宴，帝乘板輿由歸極門出，入皇極 門，至殿上降輿。
entries.en: In Longqing 4, at the suburban sacrifice completion banquet, the emperor rode a board palanquin out through the Gate of Returning to the Pole, entered through the Gate of Imperial Supremacy, and dismounted at the hall.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Longqing, when setting the suburban sacrifice completion banquet, the emperor rode a board palanquin out through the Gate of Returning to the Pole, entered through the Gate of Imperial Supremacy, and at the hall descended from the palanquin.

entries.zh: 百官乘車之制：洪武元年令，凡車不得雕飾龍鳳文。
entries.en: Regulations for officials' carriages: a Hongwu first-year order forbade dragon or phoenix ornament on any carriage.
entries.literal: Regulations for all officials' carriages: the first year of Hongwu order, all carriages were not permitted carved dragon-phoenix ornament.

entries.zh: 職官一品至三品，用間 金飾銀螭繡帶，青縵。
entries.en: Ranks one through three used awnings with gold-spaced silver chih-dragon embroidered bands and blue covers.
entries.literal: Officials of ranks one through three used spaced gold-decorated silver chih-dragon embroidered bands and blue awnings.

entries.zh: 四品五品，素獅頭繡帶，青縵。
entries.en: Ranks four and five used plain lion-head embroidered bands and blue awnings.
entries.literal: Ranks four and five, plain lion-head embroidered bands, blue awnings.

entries.zh: 六品至九品，用素雲頭青 帶，青縵。
entries.en: Ranks six through nine used plain cloud-head blue bands and blue awnings.
entries.literal: Ranks six through nine used plain cloud-head blue bands, blue awnings.

entries.zh: 轎同車制。
entries.en: Palanquins followed the same regulations as carriages.
entries.literal: Palanquins followed the carriage regulations.

entries.zh: 庶民車及轎，並用黑油，齊頭平頂，皁縵，禁用雲頭。
entries.en: Commoners' carriages and palanquins were black-lacquered with flat tops and black awnings; cloud-head ornament was forbidden.
entries.literal: Commoners' carriages and palanquins all used black oil, flush-head flat-top, black awnings; cloud-heads were forbidden.

entries.zh: 六 年令，凡車轎禁丹漆，五品以上車止用青縵。
entries.en: A sixth-year order banned cinnabar lacquer on all carriages and palanquins; carriages of the fifth rank and above were limited to blue awnings.
entries.literal: Sixth-year order: all carriages and palanquins forbade cinnabar lacquer; carriages of rank five and above used only blue awnings.

entries.zh: 婦女許坐轎，官民老疾者亦得乘之。
entries.en: Women were allowed palanquins, and aged or infirm officials and commoners could ride them as well.
entries.literal: Women were permitted to ride palanquins; officials and commoners who were old or infirm also obtained permission to ride them.

entries.zh: 景泰四年令，在京三品以上得乘轎。
entries.en: A Jingtai fourth-year order allowed officials of the third rank and above in the capital to ride palanquins.
entries.literal: Fourth year of Jingtai order: in the capital, rank three and above obtained permission to ride palanquins.

entries.zh: 弘治七年令，文武官例應乘轎者，以四人舁 之。
entries.en: A Hongzhi seventh-year order required civil and military officials entitled to palanquins to be carried by four bearers.
entries.literal: Seventh year of Hongzhi order: civil and military officials for whom palanquin riding was standard were borne by four men.

entries.zh: 其五府管事，內外鎮守、守備及公、侯、伯、都督等，不問老少，皆不得乘 轎，違例乘轎及擅用八人者，奏聞。
entries.en: Stewards of the Five Chief Offices, garrison and defense commanders, dukes, marquises, earls, and regional commanders were barred from palanquins regardless of age; violations and unauthorized use of eight bearers were reported to the throne.
entries.literal: The Five Chief Offices stewards, inner and outer garrison commanders, defense commanders, dukes, marquises, earls, regional commanders, and the like, regardless of age, all were not permitted to ride palanquins; those who violated regulations by riding palanquins or presumptuously using eight bearers were reported to the throne.

entries.zh: 蓋自太祖不欲勳臣廢騎射，雖上公，出必乘 馬。
entries.en: The founding emperor had wished to keep meritorious officials skilled in mounted archery; even the highest nobles were expected to ride when abroad.
entries.literal: This was because from the founding emperor's time he did not wish meritorious ministers to abandon mounted archery; even highest nobles, going out inevitably rode horses.

entries.zh: 永樂元年，駙馬都尉胡觀越制乘晉王濟熹朱<車尞>棕轎，爲給事中周景所劾。
entries.en: In Yongle's first year, Imperial Son-in-law Commandant Hu Guan exceeded his rank by riding Prince Ji Xi of Jin's red-framed brown palanquin and was impeached by Supervising Secretary Zhou Jing.
entries.literal: First year of Yongle, imperial son-in-law Commandant Hu Guan exceeded regulations by riding Prince Ji Xi of Jin's red-framed brown palanquin, and was impeached by Supervising Secretary Zhou Jing.

entries.zh: 有詔宥觀而賜濟熹書，切責之。
entries.en: An edict pardoned Guan but sent Ji Xi a letter of sharp rebuke.
entries.literal: There was an edict pardoning Guan and bestowing Ji Xi a letter, sternly reprimanding him.

entries.zh: 惟文職大臣乘轎，庶官亦乘馬。
entries.en: Only senior civil officials rode palanquins; lesser officials rode horses as well.
entries.literal: Only civil chief ministers rode palanquins; common officials also rode horses.

entries.zh: 又文臣皆許乘 車，大臣得乘安車。
entries.en: Civil officials were also permitted carriages, and senior ministers might ride the secure carriage.
entries.literal: Moreover all civil ministers were permitted to ride carriages; chief ministers obtained permission to ride the secure carriage.

entries.zh: 後久廢不用。
entries.en: This practice was later abandoned for a long time.
entries.literal: Later this was long abandoned and unused.

entries.zh: 正德四年，禮部侍郎劉機言，《大明集禮》， 公卿大臣得乘安車，因請定轎扇傘蓋品級等差。
entries.en: In Zhengde's fourth year, Vice Minister of Rites Liu Ji cited the Collected Rites of Great Ming, which granted secure carriages to dukes and ministers, and asked that rank gradations for palanquins, fans, parasols, and canopies be fixed.
entries.literal: Fourth year of Zhengde, Vice Minister of Rites Liu Ji spoke: the Collected Rites of Great Ming states that dukes and ministers obtain permission to ride the secure carriage; he therefore requested fixing palanquin, fan, parasol, and canopy rank gradations.

entries.zh: 帝以京城內安車傘蓋久不行，卻 其請，而命轎扇俱如例行。
entries.en: The emperor rejected the request because secure carriages, parasols, and canopies had long fallen out of use in the capital, and ordered palanquins and fans to follow ordinary practice.
entries.literal: The emperor, on the grounds that within the capital secure carriages, parasols, and canopies had long gone unpracticed, rejected his request, and ordered palanquins and fans all to follow routine practice.

entries.zh: 嘉靖十五年，禮部尚書霍韜言：「禮儀定式，京官三 品以上乘轎，邇者文官皆用肩輿，或乘女轎。
entries.en: In Jiajing's fifteenth year, Minister of Rites Huo Tao said: "The Prescribed Rites allow capital officials of the third rank and above palanquins, yet lately civil officials all use shoulder litters or women's palanquins.
entries.literal: Fifteenth year of Jiajing, Minister of Rites Huo Tao spoke: "In the Prescribed Rites, capital officials of rank three and above ride palanquins; recently civil officials all use shoulder litters, or ride women's palanquins.

entries.zh: 乞申明禮制，俾臣下有所遵守。」
entries.en: I ask that the ritual regulations be clearly restated so officials may know what to follow."
entries.literal: I beg to clarify the ritual regulations, so that ministers below may have something to observe."

entries.zh: 乃定四品下不許乘轎，亦毋得用肩輿。
entries.en: The court then barred officials below the fourth rank from palanquins and from shoulder litters as well.
entries.literal: Thereupon it was fixed that below rank four palanquins were not permitted, and shoulder litters also were not to be used.

entries.zh: 隆慶二年，給事中徐尚劾應城伯孫文棟等 乘轎出入，驕僣無狀。
entries.en: In Longqing's second year, Supervising Secretary Xu Shang impeached Yingcheng Earl Sun Wendong and others for riding palanquins in public with outrageous presumption.
entries.literal: Second year of Longqing, Supervising Secretary Xu Shang impeached Yingcheng Earl Sun Wendong and others for riding palanquins in and out, arrogant and presumptuous beyond measure.

entries.zh: 帝命奪文棟等俸。
entries.en: The emperor ordered Wendong and the others stripped of salary.
entries.literal: The emperor ordered Wendong's and the others' salaries seized.

entries.zh: 乃諭兩京武職非奉特恩不許乘轎，文官 四品以下用帷轎者，禁如例。
entries.en: Edicts to both capitals then barred military officers from palanquins unless specially favored, and forbade civil officials below the fourth rank curtained palanquins as before.
entries.literal: Thereupon an edict was issued to both capitals that military offices, unless granted special favor, were not permitted to ride palanquins; civil officials below rank four using curtained palanquins were forbidden as per precedent.

entries.zh: 萬曆三年奏定勳戚及武臣不許用帷轎、肩輿並交牀 上馬。
entries.en: In Wanli's third year it was decreed that meritorious kin and military officers might not use curtained palanquins, shoulder litters, or mounting stools to mount their horses.
entries.literal: Third year of Wanli memorial fixed that meritorious kin and military ministers were not permitted to use curtained palanquins, shoulder litters, and mounting-stool horse mounting.

entries.zh: 至若破格殊典，則宣德中少保黃淮陪遊西苑，嘗乘肩輿入禁中。
entries.en: Extraordinary exceptions did occur: during Xuande, Junior Guardian Huang Huai once rode a shoulder litter into the forbidden precinct while touring the Western Park.
entries.literal: As for violations of rank and special precedents: in Xuande's reign Junior Guardian Huang Huai accompanied tours of the Western Park and once rode a shoulder litter into the forbidden precinct.

entries.zh: 嘉靖間， 嚴嵩奉詔苑直，年及八旬，出入得乘肩輿。
entries.en: During Jiajing, Yan Song, ordered to serve at the imperial park at age eighty, was permitted a shoulder litter when coming and going.
entries.literal: During Jiajing, Yan Song received an edict to serve at the park, his years reaching eighty; going in and out he obtained permission to ride a shoulder litter.

entries.zh: 武臣則郭勳、朱希忠特命乘肩輿扈南 巡蹕，後遂賜常乘焉。
entries.en: Military officers Guo Xun and Zhu Xizhong were specially permitted shoulder litters on the southern tour, and later granted them for regular use.
entries.literal: Among military ministers Guo Xun and Zhu Xizhong were specially ordered to ride shoulder litters escorting the southern tour retinue; afterward they were granted regular use.

entries.zh: 皆非制也。
entries.en: None of these conformed to regulation.
entries.literal: All were not according to regulation.

entries.zh: 大輅 玉輅 大馬輦 小馬輦 步輦 大涼步輦 板轎 耕根車 后妃車輿 皇太子親王以下車輿 公卿以下車輿 傘蓋 鞍轡
entries.en: Great State Carriage; Jade Carriage; large and small horse sedans; hand sedans; large cool hand sedan; board palanquin; plough-root carriage; carriages for empresses and consorts; carriages for the crown prince, princes, and those below; carriages for dukes, ministers, and those below; parasols and canopies; saddles and bridles
entries.literal: Great State Carriage, Jade Carriage, Large Horse Sedan, Small Horse Sedan, Hand Sedan, Large Cool Hand Sedan, Board Palanquin, Plough-Root Carriage, Empress Consort Carriages, Crown Prince and Princes and Below Carriages, Dukes and Ministers and Below Carriages, Parasols and Canopies, Saddles and Bridles

entries.zh: 皇帝冕服：洪武元年，學士陶安請制五冕。
entries.en: On the emperor's sacrificial dress: In Hongwu 1 (1368), Academician Tao An petitioned to institute the five ceremonial caps.
entries.literal: The emperor's court robes and crown: In the first year of Hongwu, Academician Tao An requested the establishment of the five caps.

entries.zh: 太祖曰：「此禮太繁。
entries.en: The Taizu said, "This ceremony is overly elaborate.
entries.literal: The Taizu said: "This ritual is too cumbersome.

entries.zh: 祭天地、宗廟，服袞冕。
entries.en: For sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the ancestral temples, wear the full ceremonial crown and robe.
entries.literal: When sacrificing to Heaven and Earth and the ancestral temples, wear the sacrificial crown and robe.

entries.zh: 社稷等祀，服通天冠，絳紗袍。
entries.en: For rites at the altars of soil and grain and comparable ceremonies, wear the Communication-with-Heaven Cap and a deep-red gauze robe.
entries.literal: For sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain and the like, wear the Communication-with-Heaven Cap and deep-red gauze robe.

entries.zh: 餘不用。」
entries.en: The remainder are not to be used."
entries.literal: The rest are not to be used."

entries.zh: 三年，更定正旦、冬至、聖節並服袞冕，祭社稷、先農、冊拜，亦如之。
entries.en: In the third year the rule was fixed: New Year's Day, the winter solstice, and the emperor's birthday all required the full ceremonial crown and robe, and sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain, the God of Agriculture, and formal investiture audiences followed the same rule.
entries.literal: In the third year, it was revised that New Year's Day, the winter solstice, and imperial birthday all required the sacrificial crown and robe; sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain, the God of Agriculture, and investiture audiences were treated the same.

entries.zh: 十六年，定袞冕之制。
entries.en: In the sixteenth year the system for the ceremonial crown and robe was established.
entries.literal: In the sixteenth year, the regulations for the sacrificial crown and robe were fixed.

entries.zh: 冕，前圓後方，玄表纁裡。
entries.en: The crown was round in front and square behind, with a dark outer surface and deep-red lining.
entries.literal: The crown: round in front and square behind, dark on the outside and deep red within.

entries.zh: 前後各十二旒，旒五采，玉十二，珠五，採繅十有二就，就相去一寸。
entries.en: There were twelve pendants before and behind; the pendants were in five colors, with twelve jade pieces, five beads, and twelve colored silk tassels spaced one inch apart.
entries.literal: Front and rear each had twelve pendants; the pendants were five-colored; jade twelve; beads five; colored silks with twelve tassels, the tassels one inch apart.

entries.zh: 紅絲組為纓，黈纊充耳，玉簪導。
entries.en: Red silk cords formed the chin strap, yellow silk plugs filled the ears, and a jade hairpin secured the crown.
entries.literal: Red silk cords served as the chin strap; yellow silk plugs filled the ears; a jade hairpin guided it.

entries.zh: 袞，玄衣黃裳，十二章，日、月、星辰、山、龍、華蟲六章織於衣，宗彝、藻、火、粉米、黼、黻六章繡於裳。
entries.en: The sacrificial robe had a dark upper garment and yellow skirt with twelve emblems: sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and flowering creature were woven on the robe; ritual vessels, waterweed, fire, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles were embroidered on the skirt.
entries.literal: The sacrificial robe: dark upper garment and yellow lower garment, twelve emblems — sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and flowering creature, six emblems woven on the robe; ritual vessels, waterweed, fire, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles, six emblems embroidered on the skirt.

entries.zh: 白羅大帶，紅裡。
entries.en: The great belt was white gauze with a red lining.
entries.literal: A great belt of white gauze, red lining.

entries.zh: 蔽膝隨裳色，繡龍、火、山文。
entries.en: The knee cover matched the skirt in color and was embroidered with dragon, fire, and mountain motifs.
entries.literal: The knee cover followed the skirt's color, embroidered with dragon, fire, and mountain designs.

entries.zh: 玉革帶，玉佩。
entries.en: There was a leather belt set with jade and jade pendants.
entries.literal: A jade-studded leather belt and jade pendants.

entries.zh: 大綬六採，赤、黃、黑、白、縹、綠，小綬三，色同大綬。
entries.en: The great ceremonial sash used six colors—red, yellow, black, white, pale crimson, and green—with three smaller sashes in matching colors.
entries.literal: The great sash had six colors — red, yellow, black, white, pale crimson, and green; three small sashes, the colors the same as the great sash.

entries.zh: 間施三玉環。
entries.en: Three jade rings were spaced along them.
entries.literal: Three jade rings were set between them.

entries.zh: 白羅中單，黻領，青緣襈。
entries.en: The inner robe was white gauze with an opposed-triangle collar and green trim on the cuffs.
entries.literal: An inner robe of white gauze, collar with opposed-triangle pattern, green edging on the cuffs.

entries.zh: 黃襪黃舄，金飾。
entries.en: Yellow stockings and yellow court shoes were ornamented with gold.
entries.literal: Yellow stockings and yellow court shoes, with gold ornament.

entries.zh: 二十六年，更定袞冕十二章。
entries.en: In the twenty-sixth year the twelve-emblem ceremonial crown and robe were revised again.
entries.literal: In the twenty-sixth year, the sacrificial crown and robe with twelve emblems were revised.

entries.zh: 冕版廣一尺二寸，長二尺四寸。
entries.en: The crown board measured one foot two inches in width and two feet four in length.
entries.literal: The crown board was one foot two inches wide and two feet four inches long.

entries.zh: 冠上有復，玄表朱裡，餘如舊制。
entries.en: A covering was placed above the cap, dark on the outside and vermilion within; everything else followed the earlier regulations.
entries.literal: Above the cap was a covering, dark outside and vermilion within; the rest followed the old regulations.

entries.zh: 圭長一尺二寸。
entries.en: The jade tablet was one foot two inches long.
entries.literal: The tablet was one foot two inches long.

entries.zh: 袞，玄衣纁裳，十二章如舊制。
entries.en: The sacrificial robe had a dark upper garment and deep-red skirt with twelve emblems, as in the earlier regulations.
entries.literal: The sacrificial robe: dark upper garment and deep-red skirt, twelve emblems as in the old regulations.

entries.zh: 中單以素紗為之。
entries.en: The inner robe was made of plain gauze.
entries.literal: The inner robe was made of plain gauze.

entries.zh: 紅羅蔽膝，上廣一尺，下廣二尺，長三尺，織火、龍、山三章。
entries.en: The knee cover was red gauze, one foot wide at the top, two at the bottom, and three feet long, woven with the fire, dragon, and mountain emblems.
entries.literal: A knee cover of red gauze, one foot wide above, two feet wide below, three feet long, woven with fire, dragon, and mountain, three emblems.

entries.zh: 革帶佩玉，長三尺三寸。
entries.en: The leather belt bore jade pendants and was three feet three inches long.
entries.literal: A leather belt with jade pendants, three feet three inches long.

entries.zh: 大帶素表朱裡，兩邊用緣，上以朱錦，下以綠錦。
entries.en: The great belt was plain on the outside and vermilion within, with edging on both sides; vermilion brocade above and green brocade below.
entries.literal: The great belt was plain outside and vermilion within; both sides had edging; above used vermilion brocade, below used green brocade.

entries.zh: 大綬，六採
entries.en: The great ceremonial sash used six colors
entries.literal: The great sash, six colors

entries.zh: 〈（黃、白、赤、玄、縹、綠）〉
entries.en: yellow, white, red, black, pale crimson, and green.)〉
entries.literal: (yellow, white, red, black, pale crimson, green.)〉

entries.zh: 織成，純玄質五百首。
entries.en: woven to completion, of pure dark thread in five hundred tassels.
entries.literal: woven complete, pure dark substance five hundred tassels.

entries.zh: 〈（凡合單紡為一系，四系為一扶，五扶為一首。）〉
entries.en: that is, single-spun threads are combined into one strand, four strands form a tuft, and five tufts form one tassel.)〉
entries.literal: (Whenever single-spun threads are combined into one strand, four strands make one tuft, five tufts make one tassel.)〉

entries.zh: 小綬三，色同大綬。
entries.en: There were three smaller sashes in the same colors as the great sash.
entries.literal: Three small sashes, colors the same as the great sash.

entries.zh: 間織三玉環。
entries.en: Three jade rings were woven in at intervals.
entries.literal: Three jade rings were woven between them.

entries.zh: 朱襪，赤舄。
entries.en: Stockings were vermilion and court shoes red.
entries.literal: Vermilion stockings, red court shoes.

entries.zh: 永樂三年定，冕冠以皁紗為之，上復曰綖，桐板為質，衣之以綺，玄表朱裡，前圓後方。
entries.en: In Yongle 3 (1405) the regulations were set: the ceremonial crown was black gauze; the upper covering was called the tassel-band, with a paulownia core wrapped in fine silk, dark outside and vermilion within, round in front and square behind.
entries.literal: Fixed in the third year of Yongle: the ceremonial crown was made of black gauze; the upper covering was called the tassel-band; paulownia board served as the core, clothed in fine silk, dark outside and vermilion within, round in front and square behind.

entries.zh: 以玉衡維冠，玉簪貫紐，紐與冠武
entries.en: A jade crossbar held the crown in place, a jade hairpin threaded the fastening cord, and the cord and the crown's forepart
entries.literal: A jade crossbar secured the crown; a jade hairpin pierced the tie; the tie and the crown's forepart

entries.zh: 〈（足前體下曰武，綏在冠之下，亦曰武。）〉
entries.en: the portion before the feet and below the body is called the forepart, and the tassel-band beneath the crown is likewise called the forepart.)〉
entries.literal: (The portion before the feet and below the body is called the forepart; the tassel-band below the crown is also called the forepart.)〉

entries.zh: 並系纓處，皆飾以金。
entries.en: and every point where the chin strap was fastened was ornamented with gold.
entries.literal: and the places where the chin strap was attached were all ornamented with gold.

entries.zh: 綖以左右垂黈纊充耳，
entries.en: From the tassel-band yellow silk ear-plugs hung down on either side,
entries.literal: The tassel-band hung yellow silk ear-plugs to left and right,

entries.en: made of yellow jade.)〉
entries.literal: (using yellow jade.)〉

entries.zh: 系以玄紞，承以白玉瑱朱紘。
entries.en: secured with a dark cord and supported by a white-jade ear-plug on a vermilion strap.
entries.literal: attached with a dark cord, supported by a white-jade ear-plug and vermilion strap.

entries.zh: 餘如舊制。
entries.en: Everything else followed the earlier regulations.
entries.literal: The rest followed the old regulations.

entries.zh: 玉圭長一尺二寸，剡其上，刻山四，以象四鎮之山，蓋周鎮圭之制，異於大圭不瑑者也。
entries.en: The jade tablet was one foot two inches long, its upper end tapered and carved with four mountains to represent the mountains of the four quarters—essentially the Zhou quarter-tablet, unlike the great tablet, which was left uncarved.
entries.literal: The jade tablet was one foot two inches long; its top was tapered and carved with four mountains, to represent the mountains of the four quarters — this was essentially the Zhou regulation for the quarter-tablet, differing from the great tablet that was not carved.

entries.zh: 以黃綺約其下，別以囊韜之，金龍文。
entries.en: Yellow brocade bound its lower end, and a separate pouch sheathed it, ornamented with golden dragons.
entries.literal: Yellow brocade bound its lower part; separately a pouch sheathed it, with golden dragon designs.

entries.zh: 袞服十有二章。
entries.en: The sacrificial robe bore twelve emblems.
entries.literal: The sacrificial robe had twelve emblems.

entries.zh: 玄衣八章，日、月、龍在肩，星辰、山在背，火、華蟲、宗彝在袖，
entries.en: The dark upper garment bore eight emblems: sun, moon, and dragon on the shoulders; stars and mountain on the back; fire, flowering creature, and ritual vessels on the sleeves,
entries.literal: The dark upper garment had eight emblems: sun, moon, and dragon on the shoulders; stars and mountain on the back; fire, flowering creature, and ritual vessels on the sleeves,

entries.zh: 〈（每袖各三。）〉
entries.en: three on each sleeve.)〉
entries.literal: (three on each sleeve.)〉

entries.zh: 皆織成本色領褾襈裾。
entries.en: all woven in their proper colors on the collar, cuffs, edging, and hem.
entries.literal: all woven in their proper colors on collar, cuffs, edging, and hem.

entries.zh: 〈（褾者袖端。
entries.en: (The cuff is the end of the sleeve;
entries.literal: (The cuff is the sleeve end.

entries.zh: 襈者衣緣。）〉
entries.en: the edging is the border of the garment.)〉
entries.literal: The edging is the garment border.)〉

entries.zh: 纁裳四章，織藻、粉米、黼、黻各二，前三幅，後四幅，前後不相屬，共腰，有闢積，本色綼裼。
entries.en: The deep-red skirt bore four emblems—waterweed, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles, two of each—woven in three panels before and four behind, not joined front to back but sharing the waist, with a pleated fold and edging in the proper colors along the sides and hem.
entries.literal: The deep-red skirt had four emblems, woven with waterweed, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles, two each; three panels in front, four behind; front and rear not joined, sharing the waist; with a pleated fold; proper-color edging on the sides and hem.

entries.zh: 裳側有純謂之綼，裳下有純謂之裼，純者緣也。
entries.en: A border along the skirt's sides was called side-edging; a border below the skirt was called hem-edging—the term border here means edging.
entries.literal: When the skirt's sides had a border it was called side-edging; when below the skirt there was a border it was called hem-edging; border means edging.

entries.zh: 中單以素紗為之。
entries.en: The inner robe was made of plain gauze.
entries.literal: The inner robe was made of plain gauze.

entries.zh: 青領褾襈裾，領織黻文十三。
entries.en: It had a green collar, cuffs, edging, and hem, with thirteen opposed-triangle motifs woven on the collar.
entries.literal: Green collar, cuffs, edging, and hem; the collar woven with thirteen opposed-triangle designs.

entries.zh: 蔽膝隨裳色，四章，織藻、粉米、黼黻各二。
entries.en: The knee cover matched the skirt in color and bore four emblems—waterweed, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles, two of each.
entries.literal: The knee cover followed the skirt's color, four emblems, woven with waterweed, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles, two each.

entries.zh: 本色緣，有紃，施於縫中。
entries.en: It had edging in the proper colors and cords worked into the seams.
entries.literal: Proper-color edging; there were cords set within the seams.

entries.zh: 玉鉤二。
entries.en: There were two jade hooks.
entries.literal: Two jade hooks.

entries.zh: 玉佩二，各用玉珩一、瑀一、琚二、沖牙一、璜二；
entries.en: There were two jade pendants, each comprising one top bar, one secondary piece, two square plaques, one impact tooth, and two arc pieces;
entries.literal: Two jade pendants, each using one top-bar jade, one secondary jade, two square jades, one impact-tooth, and two arc jades;

entries.zh: 瑀下垂玉花一、玉滴二；
entries.en: from the secondary piece hung one jade blossom and two jade drops;
entries.literal: from the secondary jade hung one jade blossom and two jade drops;

entries.zh: 瑑飾雲龍文描金。
entries.en: They were carved with cloud-and-dragon motifs and traced in gold.
entries.literal: Carved ornament with cloud-and-dragon designs traced in gold.

entries.zh: 自珩而下系組五，貫以玉珠。
entries.en: Below the top bar five cords were fastened, strung with jade beads.
entries.literal: From the top bar downward five cords were attached, strung with jade beads.

entries.zh: 行則沖牙、二滴與璜相觸有聲。
entries.en: When the wearer walked, the impact tooth, the two drops, and the arc pieces struck one another and chimed.
entries.literal: When walking, the impact-tooth, two drops, and arc jades struck one another and made a sound.

entries.zh: 金鉤二。
entries.en: There were two gold hooks.
entries.literal: Two gold hooks.

entries.zh: 有二小綬，六採
entries.en: There were two small sashes in six colors
entries.literal: There were two small sashes, six colors

entries.zh: 〈（黃、白、赤、玄、縹、綠）〉
entries.en: yellow, white, red, black, pale crimson, and green.)〉
entries.literal: (yellow, white, red, black, pale crimson, green.)〉

entries.zh: 纁質。
entries.en: of deep-red thread.
entries.literal: of deep-red substance.

entries.zh: 大綬，六採
entries.en: The great ceremonial sash used six colors
entries.literal: The great sash, six colors

entries.zh: 〈（黃、白、赤、玄、縹、綠）〉
entries.en: yellow, white, red, black, pale crimson, and green.)〉
entries.literal: (yellow, white, red, black, pale crimson, green.)〉

entries.zh: 纁質，三小綬，色同大綬。
entries.en: of deep-red thread, with three smaller sashes in the same colors as the great sash.
entries.literal: of deep-red substance; three small sashes, colors the same as the great sash.

entries.zh: 間施三玉環，龍文，皆織成。
entries.en: Three jade rings were spaced along them, with dragon motifs, all woven to completion.
entries.literal: Three jade rings set between them, dragon designs, all woven complete.

entries.zh: 襪舄皆赤色，舄用黑絇純，以黃飾舄首。
entries.en: Stockings and court shoes were red; the shoes had black knotted trim, with yellow ornament on the toe.
entries.literal: Stockings and shoes were all red; the shoes used black knotted edging, with yellow ornament on the shoe toe.

entries.zh: 嘉靖八年，諭閣臣張璁：「袞冕有革帶，今何不用？」
entries.en: In Jiajing 8 (1529) the emperor instructed Grand Secretary Zhang Cong, "The ceremonial crown and robe include a leather belt—why is it no longer used?"
entries.literal: In the eighth year of Jiajing, the emperor instructed Grand Secretary Zhang Cong: "The sacrificial crown and robe include a leather belt — why is it not used now?"

entries.zh: 璁對曰：「按陳祥道《禮書》，古革帶、大帶，皆謂之鞶。
entries.en: Cong replied, "According to Chen Xiangdao's Book of Rites, in antiquity the leather belt and the great belt were both called the sash-girdle.
entries.literal: Cong replied: "According to Chen Xiangdao's Book of Rites, in antiquity the leather belt and great belt were both called the sash-girdle.

entries.zh: 革帶以纛佩韍，然後加以大帶，而笏搢於二帶之間。
entries.en: The leather belt carried pennants, pendants, and knee covers; only then was the great belt added, with the tablet tucked between the two belts.
entries.literal: The leather belt was used to hang pennants, pendants, and knee covers; only then was the great belt added, and the tablet inserted between the two belts.

entries.zh: 夫革帶前系韍，後系綬，左右系佩，自古冕弁恆用之。
entries.en: The leather belt fastened knee covers in front, the ceremonial sash behind, and pendants to either side; from antiquity it was always worn with the ceremonial crown and cap.
entries.literal: The leather belt attached knee covers in front, the sash behind, and pendants to left and right; from antiquity it was constantly used with the ceremonial crown and cap.

entries.zh: 今惟不用革帶，以至前後佩服皆無所繫，遂附屬裳要之間，失古制矣。」
entries.en: Today, because the leather belt is omitted, the front and rear pendants and sash have nothing to which they can be fastened and are merely attached at the skirt's waist, which departs from the ancient regulations."
entries.literal: Now only by not using the leather belt, front and rear pendants and sash have nothing to which they can be attached, and so they are made to depend on the skirt's waist — this loses the ancient regulations."

entries.zh: 帝曰：「冕服祀天地，享祖宗，若闕革帶，非齊明盛服之意。
entries.en: The emperor said, "The ceremonial robes are worn to sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and to offer to the ancestors; to omit the leather belt is not in keeping with the intent of pure and splendid full dress.
entries.literal: The emperor said: "The court robes and crown sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and offer to the ancestors; if the leather belt is lacking, this is not the meaning of pure and splendid full dress.

entries.zh: 及觀《會典》載蔽膝用羅，上織火、山、龍三章，並大帶緣用錦，皆與今所服不合。
entries.en: Moreover, the Collected Statutes record that the knee cover was gauze woven with the fire, mountain, and dragon emblems, and that the great belt's edging was brocade—all unlike what is worn today.
entries.literal: Moreover, on examining the Collected Statutes, it records that the knee cover used gauze with fire, mountain, and dragon, three emblems woven above, and that the great belt's edging used brocade — all unlike what is worn today.

entries.zh: 卿可並革帶系蔽膝、佩、綬之式，詳考繪圖以進。」
entries.en: You should also investigate in detail how the leather belt fastened the knee cover, pendants, and sash, draw illustrations, and submit them."
entries.literal: You may together with the leather belt's manner of attaching knee cover, pendants, and sash, investigate in detail, draw illustrations, and submit them."

entries.zh: 又云：「衣裳分上下服，而今衣恆掩裳。
entries.en: He also said, "The upper garment and skirt are distinct upper and lower garments, yet today the robe constantly covers the skirt.
entries.literal: He also said: "Upper garment and skirt are separate upper and lower dress, yet today the robe constantly covers the skirt.

entries.zh: 裳制如帷，而今兩幅。
entries.en: The skirt should be shaped like a curtain, yet today it is made in two panels.
entries.literal: The skirt's form should be like a curtain, yet today there are two panels.

entries.zh: 朕意衣但當與裳要下齊，而露裳之六章，何如？」
entries.en: My thought is that the robe should end only at the skirt's waist, leaving the skirt's six emblems visible—what do you think?"
entries.literal: My idea is that the robe should only come level with the skirt's waist below, while revealing the skirt's six emblems — what do you think?"

entries.zh: 已，又諭璁以變更祖制為疑。
entries.en: Shortly afterward he again expressed to Cong his concern about altering the ancestral regulations.
entries.literal: Thereafter he again instructed Cong, expressing doubt about altering the ancestral regulations.

entries.zh: 璁對曰：「臣考禮制，衣不掩裳，與聖意允合。
entries.en: Cong replied, "Your subject has examined the ritual regulations: the robe does not cover the skirt, which fully accords with Your Majesty's intent.
entries.literal: Cong replied: "Your subject has examined the ritual regulations: the robe does not cover the skirt — this fully accords with Your Majesty's intent.

entries.zh: 夫衣六章，裳六章，義各有取，衣自不容掩裳。
entries.en: The robe bears six emblems and the skirt six, each with its own significance; the robe by its nature cannot cover the skirt.
entries.literal: The robe has six emblems, the skirt six emblems; each has its own meaning — the robe by nature cannot cover the skirt.

entries.zh: 《大明集禮》及《會典》與古制不異。
entries.en: The Collected Rites of the Great Ming and the Collected Statutes agree with the ancient regulations.
entries.literal: The Collected Rites of the Great Ming and the Collected Statutes do not differ from the ancient regulations.

entries.zh: 今衣八章，裳四章，故衣常掩裳，然於典籍無所準。
entries.en: Today the robe has eight emblems and the skirt four, so the robe constantly covers the skirt—yet this has no basis in the canonical texts.
entries.literal: Now the robe has eight emblems and the skirt four, so the robe constantly covers the skirt — yet this has no basis in the canonical texts.

entries.zh: 內閣所藏圖注，蓋因官司織造，循習訛謬。
entries.en: The illustrated commentaries kept in the Grand Secretariat probably reflect errors introduced when the official workshops wove the garments and followed corrupted practice.
entries.literal: The illustrated commentaries kept in the Grand Secretariat were probably because the official workshops wove them, following corrupted practice.

entries.zh: 今訂正之，乃復祖制，非有變更。」
entries.en: To correct this now is to restore the ancestral regulations, not to alter them."
entries.literal: To correct this now is to restore the ancestral regulations, not to make a change."

entries.zh: 帝意乃決。
entries.en: The emperor's mind was made up.
entries.literal: The emperor's mind was then decided.

entries.zh: 因復諭璁曰：「衣有六章，古以繪，今當以織。
entries.en: He then again told Cong, "The robe has six emblems; in antiquity they were painted, but today they should be woven.
entries.literal: He then again instructed Cong: "The robe has six emblems; in antiquity they were painted — today they should be woven.

entries.zh: 朕命織染局考國初冕服，日月各徑五寸，當從之。
entries.en: I have ordered the Weaving and Dyeing Bureau to consult the founding-era court robes and crown: the sun and moon each measured five inches across, and that measure should be restored.
entries.literal: I command the Weaving and Dyeing Bureau to examine the court robes and crown of the dynasty's founding; the sun and moon each had a diameter of five inches — this should be followed.

entries.zh: 裳六章，古用繡，亦當從之。
entries.en: The skirt bore six emblems, and in antiquity they were embroidered; that practice should be followed as well.
entries.literal: The skirt had six emblems; antiquity used embroidery — this too should be followed.

entries.zh: 古色用玄黃，取象天地。
entries.en: In antiquity the colors were dark and yellow, taking Heaven and Earth as their model.
entries.literal: In antiquity the colors used were dark and yellow, taking the image of Heaven and Earth.

entries.zh: 今裳用纁，於義無取，當從古。
entries.en: Today the skirt is deep-red, which carries no proper symbolic meaning; we should return to the ancient practice.
entries.literal: Today the skirt uses deep-red — in meaning there is nothing to be taken from this; we should follow antiquity.

entries.zh: 革帶即束帶，後當用玉，以佩綬系之於下。
entries.en: The leather belt is the waist belt; jade should be used on it, with pendants and the ceremonial sash fastened below.
entries.literal: The leather belt is the waist belt; afterward jade should be used, with pendants and sash attached below it.

entries.zh: 蔽膝隨裳色，其繡上龍下火，可不用山。
entries.en: The knee cover should match the skirt in color, embroidered with a dragon above and fire below; the mountain emblem may be omitted.
entries.literal: The knee cover follows the skirt's color; its embroidery has a dragon above and fire below — the mountain need not be used.

entries.zh: 卿與內閣諸臣同考之。」
entries.en: You and the other ministers of the Grand Secretariat should investigate this together."
entries.literal: You and the various ministers of the Grand Secretariat should examine this together."

entries.zh: 於是楊一清等詳議：「袞冕之服，自黃、虞以來，玄衣黃裳，為十二章。
entries.en: Thereupon Yang Yiqing and others submitted a detailed memorial: "From the age of the Yellow Emperor and Shun onward, the sacrificial crown and robe consisted of a dark upper garment and yellow skirt bearing twelve emblems.
entries.literal: Thereupon Yang Yiqing and others deliberated in detail: "From the Yellow Emperor and Shun onward, the sacrificial crown and robe had a dark upper garment and yellow skirt, making twelve emblems.

entries.zh: 日、月、星辰、山、龍、華蟲，其序自上而下，為衣之六章；
entries.en: The sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and flowering creature, ordered from top to bottom, formed the robe's six emblems;
entries.literal: Sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and flowering creature — their order from top to bottom were the six emblems of the robe;

entries.zh: 宗彝、藻、火、粉米、黼、黻，其序自下而上，為裳之六章。
entries.en: ritual vessels, waterweed, fire, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles, ordered from bottom to top, formed the skirt's six emblems.
entries.literal: ritual vessels, waterweed, fire, millet grain, axe-and-gouge, and opposed triangles — their order from bottom to top were the six emblems of the skirt.

entries.zh: 自周以後浸，變其制，或八章，或九章，已戾於古矣。
entries.en: From the Zhou onward the regulations were gradually altered, sometimes to eight emblems and sometimes to nine, already straying from antiquity.
entries.literal: From Zhou onward they gradually changed the regulations, sometimes to eight emblems, sometimes nine — already departing from antiquity.

entries.zh: 我太祖皇帝復定為十二章之制，司造之官仍習舛訛，非製作之初意。
entries.en: Our Founding Emperor restored the twelve-emblem system, yet the workshops charged with production still followed corrupted practice, contrary to the original intent.
entries.literal: Our Founding Emperor restored the twelve-emblem regulation, but the officials who made them still followed corrupted errors — not the original intent of manufacture.

entries.zh: 伏乞聖斷不疑。」
entries.en: We humbly beg Your Majesty to decide without hesitation."
entries.literal: We humbly beg Your Sacred judgment without doubt."

entries.zh: 帝乃令擇吉更正其制。
entries.en: The emperor then ordered an auspicious day chosen for correcting the regulations.
entries.literal: The emperor then ordered an auspicious day chosen to correct the regulations.

entries.zh: 冠以圓匡烏紗冒之，旒綴七採玉珠十二，青纊充耳，綴玉珠二，餘如舊制。
entries.en: The crown had a round frame covered with black gauze; the tassels carried twelve beads in seven colors; blue stuffing filled the ears, with two jade beads attached; everything else followed the earlier regulations.
entries.literal: The crown had a round frame covered with black gauze; the tassels strung twelve beads of seven colors; blue stuffing filled the ears, with two jade beads attached; the rest followed the old regulations.

entries.zh: 玄衣黃裳，衣裳各六章。
entries.en: There was a dark upper garment and a yellow skirt, the robe and skirt each bearing six emblems.
entries.literal: Dark upper garment, yellow skirt — robe and skirt each six emblems.

entries.zh: 洪武間舊制，日月徑五寸，裳前後連屬如帷，六章用繡。
entries.en: Under the old Hongwu regulations, the sun and moon measured five inches across; the skirt was joined front and back like a curtain, and the six emblems were embroidered.
entries.literal: Under the Hongwu old regulations, sun and moon had a diameter of five inches; the skirt front and back were continuous like a curtain; the six emblems used embroidery.

entries.zh: 蔽膝隨裳色，羅為之，上繡龍一，下繡火三，系於革帶，大帶素表朱裡，上緣以朱，下以綠。
entries.en: The knee cover matched the skirt in color and was made of gauze, with one dragon embroidered above and three fires below, fastened to the leather belt; the great belt was plain outside and vermilion within, edged in vermilion above and green below.
entries.literal: The knee cover followed the skirt's color, made of gauze, one dragon embroidered above and three fires below, attached to the leather belt; the great belt was plain outside and vermilion inside, with vermilion edging above and green below.

entries.zh: 革帶前用玉，其後無玉，以佩綬系而掩之。
entries.en: The leather belt bore jade in front but not behind, with pendants and sash attached to cover the rear.
entries.literal: The leather belt had jade in front but none behind; pendants and sash were fastened to cover it.

entries.zh: 中單及圭，俱如永樂間制。
entries.en: The inner robe and jade tablet both followed the Yongle regulations.
entries.literal: The inner robe and tablet were both as under the Yongle regulations.

entries.zh: 朱襪，赤舄，黃條緣玄纓結。
entries.en: There were vermilion stockings and red court shoes, with yellow stripe edging and dark knotted laces.
entries.literal: Vermilion stockings, red shoes, with yellow stripe edging and dark laces knotted.

entries.zh: 皇帝通天冠服：洪武元年定，郊廟、省牲，皇太子諸王冠婚、醮戒，則服通天冠、絳紗袍。
entries.en: The emperor's Communication-with-Heaven Cap dress was fixed in Hongwu 1 (1368). For suburban temples, inspection of sacrificial animals, the crown prince's and princes' capping and wedding rites, and fasting consecration, he wore the Communication-with-Heaven Cap and a deep-red gauze robe.
entries.literal: The emperor's Communication-with-Heaven Cap dress: fixed in Hongwu 1; for suburban temples, inspecting sacrificial animals, crown prince and princes' capping and wedding, and fasting consecration, one wore the Communication-with-Heaven Cap and deep-red gauze robe.

entries.zh: 冠加金博山，附蟬十二，首施珠翠，黑介幘，組纓，玉簪導。
entries.en: The cap bore a gold Mount Bo ornament, twelve cicada pins, pearls and kingfisher feathers on the front, a black cap covering, cord tassels, and a jade hairpin guide.
entries.literal: The crown was topped with a gold Mount Bo, twelve cicadas attached, pearls and kingfisher feathers set on the front, a black cap covering, cord tassels, and a jade hairpin guide.

entries.zh: 絳紗袍，深衣制。
entries.en: The deep-red gauze robe followed the deep-garment cut.
entries.literal: Deep-red gauze robe, in deep-garment style.

entries.zh: 白紗內單，皁領褾襈裾。
entries.en: There was a white gauze inner robe with a black collar, cuffs, edging, and hem.
entries.literal: White gauze inner robe, with black collar, cuffs, edging, and hem.

entries.zh: 絳紗蔽膝，白假帶，方心曲領。
entries.en: There was a deep-red gauze knee cover, a white false belt, and a square-hearted curved collar.
entries.literal: Deep-red gauze knee cover, white false belt, square heart and curved collar.

entries.zh: 白襪，赤舄。
entries.en: White stockings and red court shoes completed the dress.
entries.literal: White stockings, red shoes.

entries.zh: 其革帶、佩綬，與袞服同。
entries.en: The leather belt and pendant sash were the same as those worn with the sacrificial robe.
entries.literal: Its leather belt and pendant sash were the same as for the sacrificial robe.

entries.zh: 皇帝常服：洪武三年定，烏紗折角向上巾，盤領窄袖袍，束帶間用金、琥珀、透犀。
entries.en: The emperor's daily dress was fixed in Hongwu 3 (1370): a black gauze cap with upturned corners, a round-collared narrow-sleeved robe, and a waist belt sometimes set with gold, amber, and transparent rhinoceros horn.
entries.literal: The emperor's daily dress: fixed in Hongwu 3 — black gauze cap with corners folded upward, round-collar narrow-sleeved robe, waist belt sometimes using gold, amber, and transparent rhinoceros horn.

entries.zh: 永樂三年更定，冠以烏紗冒之，折角向上，其後名翼善冠。
entries.en: It was revised in Yongle 3 (1405): the cap was covered with black gauze and folded upward at the corners, and afterward was named the Beneficent-Wing Cap.
entries.literal: Revised in Yongle 3: the cap was covered with black gauze with corners folded upward; afterward it was named the Beneficent-Wing Cap.

entries.zh: 袍黃，盤領，窄袖，前後及兩肩各織金盤龍一。
entries.en: The robe was yellow, with a round collar and narrow sleeves; one gold coiled dragon was woven on the front, back, and each shoulder.
